Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient was also directly physically injured; that direct-injury theme is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Threat items center on personal physical danger and hypervigilance in the environment ('back to wall', exaggerated startle), which fits direct personal assault/combat trauma more than trauma to a loved one, and is not well linked to the reported appraisal content.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, this item implies an ongoing need to guard against immediate external danger to oneself. That does not fit well with the rest of the profile, which centers on bereavement-related cognitions (survival guilt, numbness) rather than personal threat exposure. It is also weakly aligned with the formulation, where Threat is linked mainly with Negative Appraisals and not with trigger-driven hyperarousal or ongoing danger monitoring.

The threat items are dominated by nonspecific hyperarousal and reminder reactivity, which usually implies trigger-linked activation, but the formulation specifies Triggers → Threat as inactive. With no trigger content present, 'physical reactions when reminded' is poorly aligned with the stated formulation structure.

'Mistrust: People can't be trusted' is a broad interpersonal appraisal that is not well anchored to trauma to a loved one in the rest of this profile. The other appraisal items center on guilt and emotional deadness, but pervasive mistrust suggests a different trauma pattern and lacks support from the selected threat items.

vignette:
Somchai is a 60-year-old married Southeast Asian American fisherman who came to treatment after years of trying to keep his distress contained within the routines of work and home. He speaks about the defining event in a flat, careful way at first, but the details are vivid. He and a loved one had been out on the water together when conditions changed quickly. What had started as ordinary work became a scene of confusion, shouting, and helplessness. He remembers the movement of the boat turning violent, the sound of water striking the hull, and the moment he understood that the person beside him was in grave danger. He survived. His loved one did not. What stays with him is not only the loss itself but the unbearable fact that he was there, that he came back, and that the other person did not. He has come to believe there is something deeply wrong in that outcome, and when he says, “It should have been me too,” he does not mean it dramatically. He means it as a settled truth.

In the weeks after the death, Somchai returned to fishing because it was how he had always supported his family and because staying home felt impossible. Yet the work environment itself was full of moments that struck him without warning. The slap of waves against the boat, a sudden shift in weather, the smell of the water before dawn, even the jolt of the engine could bring on an immediate bodily reaction. His chest would tighten, his heart would pound, and his hands would go cold or start to shake. At those moments he did not simply remember what happened; his body reacted as if it were meeting the danger again. He became frightened of how quickly this could happen, especially while working with other men on the boat, where he felt he had to remain steady and competent.

Alongside this, strong feelings would surge up with little room between them: fear when the water turned rough, anger that the loss had happened at all, shame when he saw himself as the one who returned, and guilt so sharp it could leave him silent for hours afterward. He does not talk easily about these emotions at home. His wife has noticed that he can sit through dinner saying almost nothing, staring at a fixed point as if he is somewhere else. Somchai describes this less as sadness than as feeling “dead inside,” as though whatever was warm or responsive in him went quiet after the death. He still does what needs to be done, but he no longer feels present in the same way with his family. He recognizes that his wife wants comfort and closeness from him, and he hates that he often has nothing to give.

Over time he also came to see other people differently. He is wary with neighbors, guarded with other fishermen, and reluctant to rely on anyone. He speaks as though trust itself has become unsafe. Even ordinary offers of help can feel suspect to him, and he keeps his thoughts to himself because he is certain people cannot really be trusted. This has narrowed his world. On the docks he keeps conversations brief. He avoids lingering after work. He has become known as more distant than he used to be, something that troubles his wife but that Somchai experiences as necessary self-protection.

His nights are especially difficult. He lies awake long after going to bed, his mind tense and his body unable to settle. On other nights he falls asleep only to wake again, alert and exhausted at once. He dreads the long dark hours because there is nothing to distract him from the loss or from the thought that he should not be the one still here. By morning he is worn down, and the fatigue follows him onto the boat, where the physical demands of fishing only sharpen his sense of strain.

What finally brought Somchai to seek help was not a new trauma but the accumulation of these years: the way his body still reacts on the water, the distance his wife feels from him, the exhaustion of broken sleep, and the conviction that he has not truly come back from that day even though his life kept moving forward. He arrived for treatment with little expectation that talking would change much. At the same time, beneath his guardedness, he carries a quiet hope that he might find a way to live with the loss without feeling so hollow, and a fear that if nothing changes, the rest of his life will remain organized around that single day on the water.
